title: Khadur Sahib
hookLine: where Guru Angad taught the script

lines: A WOODEN BOARD, A REED PEN.
cards: How did a child in Punjab learn to write before notebooks were cheap? On a wooden board about the size of a schoolbook, smeared with a pale clay wash and dried in the sun.
The child dips a reed pen in ink and writes letters, round and careful. When the board is full, it's washed clean, and the child starts again.

Boards like this, called takhtis, are an old way of learning to write in Punjab. And Sikh tradition remembers a Guru who sat with children and their letters, in a small town near the Beas river: Khadur Sahib.

teach.b: First, the Guru. Khadur was the town of Guru Angad, the second Guru, who took up the work after Guru Nanak. Tradition says he spent his days there among the sangat, with special care for teaching.
Tradition says Guru Angad shaped and taught the letters now called Gurmukhi, and wrote out simple primers so children, and grown-ups too, could read the Guru's word for themselves.
The Guru Granth Sahib is written in Gurmukhi to this day, so when a Sikh child learns to read Gurbani, the line of teaching runs back, in Sikh memory, to a teacher sitting with children here.
Third, the alphabet as a teaching. Guru Nanak had already written a hymn on the letters, the Patti, in which, in paraphrase, each letter becomes a lesson about God and the self.
Learning letters and learning the path were never two separate things.
Fourth, the kitchen next door. The Guru Granth Sahib, in a ballad of the musicians Satta and Balwand, praises Mata Khivi, Guru Angad's wife.

In paraphrase, she was a good woman whose shade was wide and leafy, and in her langar, rice pudding with ghee was handed out to all. So Khadur Sahib holds both: letters for the mind, and food for anyone who came.
Today the town keeps gurdwaras that remember Guru Angad, and children still learn their letters from the same alphabet.

how: Sikhs visit Khadur Sahib to remember Guru Angad and Mata Khivi, and Sikh children learn to read Gurbani in the Gurmukhi script, often starting with the alphabet at a gurdwara Punjabi class.

games.why: tradition says Guru Angad shaped and taught the Gurmukhi letters and wrote primers, so anyone could read the Guru's word.

practice: With a pen on scrap paper, or a finger on your palm, write one letter slowly: the first letter of your name, or the first Gurmukhi letter, oora, a little curl with a tail.
Breathe out as you write it, and notice the shape and the turn. Then rub it out, the way a child washes the board, and write it once more.

wordCard.voice: Khadur Sahib. The town of Guru Angad, where tradition says he taught the Gurmukhi letters, and where Mata Khivi's langar fed all who came. Today's word.
